html:
The Poverty Point culture was a society of the lower Mississippi valley and the nearby Gulf coast, from about 1730 to 1350 BCE. The map shows it in 1500 BCE. It is named after its great site of Poverty Point in northeast Louisiana.

At Poverty Point, people raised six concentric C-shaped ridges of earth and several large mounds, one of the biggest earthworks in North America at the time. Unusually, they did this as hunters, fishers and gatherers, not farmers. Rivers and wetlands fed them well enough.

The site was also a trade hub. Copper from the Great Lakes, stone from the Ohio valley and the Appalachians, and lead ore reached it from hundreds of kilometres away. Thousands of fired clay balls, used to cook food in earth ovens, are a trademark of the culture.

Earlier mound building at Watson Brake shows the tradition is even older. Poverty Point came long before the Adena, Hopewell and Mississippian mound builders. UNESCO listed it in 2014.
